Threat.value: Having strong negative feelings such as fear, horror, anger, guilt, or shame
I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
Fragments of the memory appear suddenly without warning and then disappear
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it

Negative Appraisals.value: My life has been destroyed by the trauma
I have to be on guard all the time

issues.explanation: 'Shouting in Arabic' is hard to reconcile with the validated trauma type of stalking unless there is specific trauma detail indicating the stalker used Arabic; with the rest of the profile, this trigger appears overly specific and disconnected from the other stalking-related items.

issues.item: Memory: Verbal Access: I can talk about what happened very easily.
issues.explanation: 'I can talk about what happened very easily' conflicts with the same Memory node items describing fragmented, intrusive, partially inaccessible trauma memory ('extremely clear while others are completely blank' and 'fragments appear suddenly without warning'). While not impossible, this is a direct enough tension within the node to question coherence.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: Fear of losing control of anger and doing something terrible is poorly integrated with the rest of the profile, which centers on fear, mistrust, stranger threat, and life damage after stalking. It points toward a perpetration/harm-to-others concern not otherwise represented in Threat, Triggers, Memory, or strategies, making the formulation less coherent.

vignette:
Maren Holst is a 28-year-old elementary school teacher of Norwegian descent who presented for psychological assessment following a prolonged period of stalking that began approximately fourteen months ago. She lives with her long-term partner in a mid-sized city and had, by all accounts, built a life she found genuinely satisfying - a stable classroom, a close circle of friends, a relationship she described as grounding. That sense of safety collapsed incrementally over the course of nearly five months, during which a former acquaintance pursued her with an escalating persistence that moved from unwanted messages to physical surveillance of her home, her school, and her daily routes.

The stalking did not announce itself as dangerous all at once. It began with texts she dismissed as awkward, then progressed to appearances she told herself were coincidences. The moment that seems to have lodged most deeply occurred on a Tuesday evening when Maren was locking up her classroom after an after-school meeting. The hallway was empty and unusually quiet - that particular, pressurised silence of a building that has just exhaled its last occupants - when she became aware of breathing behind her. Close, deliberate, unhurried. She turned to find the man standing less than two metres away, watching her. He said nothing. The encounter lasted perhaps twenty seconds before he walked away, but in those seconds Maren found herself entirely unable to speak, her body rigid, her mind producing no coherent language for what was happening. She eventually called the police, and their arrival - officers asking her to recount events she could not sequence, pressing for details she could not locate - left her feeling exposed and disbelieved rather than protected.

The stalking was eventually addressed through a restraining order, but the legal resolution brought Maren little relief. In the months that followed, her experience of the world reorganised itself around a set of signals she had learned, in the most visceral way, to treat as warnings. The sound of heavy breathing - a colleague with a cold, a child running in from recess - would stop her mid-sentence, her attention seized and narrowed. Unusual quiet in the school corridors, the kind that falls between bells, would send a cold alertness through her that she could not talk herself out of. She had come to believe that silence of that quality was not neutral; it was the moment before something happened. She began scanning hallways before entering them, positioning herself in her classroom so that she could see the door at all times, and tracking the movements of anyone who lingered near the school entrance.

Strangers approaching her in ordinary situations - a parent wanting to introduce themselves, a colleague she hadn't met - registered in her body as threat before her mind could intervene. She had come to understand people, broadly, as individuals whose intentions could not be assumed benign. When police cars appeared in her vicinity, even parked and unattended, she felt a complicated wash of fear and something closer to shame, a re-experiencing of the night she had stood in that hallway unable to adequately explain what had happened to her. She had come to feel, with a certainty that resisted contradiction, that her life as she had imagined it was no longer available to her.

Her memory of the stalking period is fragmented in a way she finds deeply disorienting. Certain moments are rendered in her mind with almost unbearable clarity - the texture of the hallway floor, the precise quality of that silence - while other stretches are simply absent. Fragments surface without invitation and then vanish before she can examine them. When she attempts to describe her experience to her partner, she finds herself stranded mid-sentence, aware of what she knows but unable to produce words adequate to it. This has placed a quiet but accumulating strain on the relationship she once described as her anchor.

What finally brought Maren to seek help was a parent-teacher evening three weeks ago, during which she found herself unable to remain in the room when a father she did not recognise walked in late and stood near the back. She left her own classroom, stood in the corridor, and wept. What she most fears, she said at intake, is that this is simply who she is now. What she most hopes is that she is wrong.
